title: 🔌 MCP & CONTEXT ENGINEERING
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD → then expand → grade what you missed.
⭐ = decides the round. 🔥 = trending 2026. 📍 = you were asked this. 📝 = no vault note yet.

♻️ Merged 19 Sep 2026: the MCP / A2A / context-engineering / prompt-versioning questions from jbtiq_agentic.md and jbtiq_llm.md were folded into #1, #6, #14 and #22 as 🗣️ Phrasing drill blocks (those drill files are retired).

questions.text: What is MCP and what problem does it actually solve?
points: Open protocol standardising how models reach tools, data and prompts — JSON-RPC over a defined transport
The problem was M×N: every model host × every integration, hand-wired. MCP makes it M+N
Server exposes capability; client (the model host) consumes — clean separation of who owns what
Value is ecosystem, not capability — you could always call an API; now the integration is portable
Think "USB-C for model integrations" — one connector, many peripherals
questions.badge: Trending — MCP questions now recur across agentic JDs + LeetCode Discuss (2025–26)
questions.flow: M×N integrations → standard protocol → servers expose, hosts consume → portability is the win
questions.trap: describing it as a new way to do function calling — function calling is the model feature, MCP is the plumbing standard

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_agentic Q12: "What problem does MCP actually solve, and what are the moving parts — host, client, server?"
drill.badge: Trending — MCP questions now recur across agentic JDs + LeetCode Discuss (2025–26)
drill.hint: Before MCP, connecting M apps to N tools cost how many integrations? Then name who runs where.
points: The problem is M×N integration sprawl: every AI app hand-wiring every tool/data source. MCP standardizes the interface so a tool integration is written once as a server and any MCP-capable app consumes it — M+N instead of M×N, "USB-C for AI context" is the honest analogy.

Topology: the host is the AI application embedding the LLM (IDE, chat app, agent runtime); it runs an MCP client per connection; servers expose capabilities over JSON-RPC via stdio (local) or streamable HTTP (remote).

The three primitives to name: tools (model-invoked actions), resources (application-controlled context/data), prompts (user-invoked templates) — the distinction of who controls invocation is the design insight people miss.

Architect's reading: MCP turns integrations into a market of interchangeable capability servers — internal platform teams ship one server per system of record, every agent product in the org consumes it; governance (authn, permissions, audit) concentrates at the protocol boundary.

Balance to voice: a remote MCP server is a new trust boundary — a malicious or compromised server injects content straight into agent context, so server provenance and permissioning become supply-chain concerns.
drill.oneLiner: MCP collapses M×N integrations to M+N by standardizing how hosts discover and invoke external capabilities — tools, resources and prompts served over JSON-RPC — and its architectural payoff is that governance and reuse concentrate at one protocol boundary.

questions.text: What are the MCP primitives?
points: Tools — model-invoked actions, side effects expected (the familiar one)
Resources — application-controlled context the host can read: files, records, docs. Not model-invoked
Prompts — user-invoked templates/workflows the server offers
The distinction is who initiates: model (tools) · app (resources) · user (prompts)
Sampling lets a server ask the client's model for a completion — inverts the usual direction
questions.flow: tools = model-initiated · resources = app-initiated · prompts = user-initiated · sampling inverts it
questions.trap: treating everything as a tool — resources exist so context doesn't have to be fetched by tool call

questions.text: How does a client actually connect?
points: stdio — local subprocess, simplest, trust follows the process boundary
Streamable HTTP (superseded HTTP+SSE) — remote servers, sessions, resumability
Lifecycle: initialise → capability negotiation → operate → shut down
Capability negotiation is why version skew is survivable — both sides declare what they support
Remote transport is where authn/authz and network trust become your problem
questions.flow: stdio local · streamable HTTP remote → initialise → negotiate capabilities → operate
questions.trap: assuming remote MCP inherits the local trust model

questions.text: Why should an architect care? Isn't this just an SDK detail?
points: Decouples capability from host — swap Claude/GPT/an internal model without rewriting integrations
Turns integrations into independently versioned, independently owned services — team boundaries, not a monolith of tools
Enables an internal capability registry: teams publish servers, agents discover them
Reduces vendor lock-in at the integration layer, which is where lock-in actually hurts
Cost: another network hop, another thing to secure, version management across servers
questions.flow: capability decoupled from host → integrations become owned services → registry + reuse → lock-in drops
questions.trap: pitching it as a productivity library rather than an architectural boundary

questions.text: Would you build a server or consume one?
points: Consume for commodity integrations — GitHub, Slack, Postgres; don't rebuild what exists
Build for proprietary domain capability: your data, your business actions, your compliance rules
Building means owning: auth, rate limits, versioning, audit, and the security review
Third-party servers are supply chain — a server you install can read what you connect to it (#8)
Middle path most teams land on: consume commodity, build a thin internal server over your own domain
questions.flow: commodity → consume · proprietary domain → build → but building means owning auth, versioning, audit
questions.trap: installing community servers into a production agent with no review

questions.text: MCP and A2A — same thing?
points: MCP = agent ↔ tools/context. Vertical: how one agent reaches capability
A2A = agent ↔ agent. Horizontal: discovery, task delegation, negotiation between peers
Complementary, not competing — an A2A-reachable agent still uses MCP internally
A2A adds: agent cards for discovery, task lifecycle, opaque agents (you don't see internals)
Both are young — say clearly which parts are stable and which are still moving
questions.badge: Evergreen (the comparative form is how it's asked)
questions.flow: MCP vertical to tools · A2A horizontal between agents → complementary layers
questions.trap: presenting them as alternatives to choose between

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_agentic Q13: "MCP vs A2A vs plain function calling — draw the boundaries. When is each the right layer?"
drill.badge: Evergreen (the comparative form is how it's asked)
drill.hint: One connects a model to capabilities, one connects peers to each other, one is just the model-vendor API primitive. What changes at each boundary?
points: Function calling is the model-API primitive: schemas in, structured call out, you execute. It's within one application; no discovery, no transport, no interop — the atom everything else is built from.
MCP standardizes the agent↔capability boundary: how one application discovers and invokes external tools/data. The consumer is a model runtime; the relationship is client-server.

A2A-style protocols target the agent↔agent boundary: opaque peers exchanging tasks and results with capability discovery, long-running task lifecycle, and no obligation to expose internals — the relationship is peer delegation across trust domains (different teams, different vendors).

The clean mental model: MCP is how an agent uses tools; A2A is how an agent delegates work to another autonomous system. A tool is transparent and stateless-ish; a peer agent has its own policy, state, and failure modes.

Practical status check to voice: MCP has broad adoption momentum; agent-to-agent interop is younger and consolidating — commit hard to the tool boundary, keep the agent-peer boundary abstracted, and don't bet the architecture on any single interop spec yet.
drill.oneLiner: Function calling is the in-app primitive, MCP standardizes agent-to-capability, A2A-class protocols standardize agent-to-agent delegation across trust domains — I commit to the tool boundary and keep peer-agent interop behind an abstraction.

questions.text: You already have OpenAPI. Why add MCP?
points: OpenAPI describes an HTTP API for developers; MCP describes capability for a model, with the host relationship built in
MCP carries what OpenAPI doesn't: resources, prompts, sampling, negotiated capabilities, a session
OpenAPI specs are usually far too granular and too numerous to hand a model directly (06-AGENTIC-AI #7)
Perfectly valid to wrap an OpenAPI surface in a small MCP server that exposes intention-shaped tools
Not either/or: OpenAPI stays the contract between services, MCP is the contract with the model
questions.flow: OpenAPI = dev contract · MCP = model contract → wrap, don't replace → curate granularity in the wrapper
questions.trap: auto-generating one MCP tool per OpenAPI operation — you've moved the problem, not solved it

questions.text: What's the security model?
points: MCP is a transport standard, not a security model — authn/authz is yours to impose
Threats: malicious server · tool poisoning (hostile text in a tool description) · confused deputy · token passthrough · cross-server data exfiltration
The agent's identity must not be the user's identity — scope credentials per server, per tool
Every tool call is untrusted input and a privileged action (06-AGENTIC-AI #18): approval gates on destructive ops
Audit every invocation: who, what, on whose behalf, with what result
questions.flow: protocol ≠ security → scope creds per server → treat descriptions as untrusted → gate destructive → audit all
questions.trap: trusting a server's tool descriptions — they enter your model's context as instructions

questions.text: Design an MCP server over our internal systems.
points: Start from user intentions, not from your service catalogue — one tool per thing someone wants done
Coarse and few beats thin and many; each description is prompt budget you pay every call
Return model-shaped output: compact, structured, self-describing; never a raw 400-field payload
Auth per call carrying the real principal; enforce authorisation server-side, never trust the caller's claim
Bake in idempotency, timeouts, pagination and clear errors — the model retries (06-AGENTIC-AI #8)
questions.flow: intentions → few coarse tools → compact structured returns → per-call authz → idempotent + bounded
questions.trap: mirroring your microservice boundaries into tool boundaries

questions.text: We're a Spring shop. What does this look like in Java?
points: Spring AI MCP — server and client starters; annotate methods as tools, schema derived from types
Same discipline as 03-JAVA-SPRING #38: intention-shaped tools, per-call authz, approval on destructive
Existing Spring assets carry over directly: Security for authn, Actuator for health, Micrometer for tracing
Deploy an MCP server like any other Boot service — same CI, same rollout, same on-call
Contract versioning is the new discipline: a tool signature change is a breaking API change
questions.flow: Boot starter → annotated tools → schema from types → reuse Security/Actuator/Micrometer → version the tool contract
questions.trap: treating an MCP server as a script rather than a production service with an API contract

questions.text: Ten MCP servers, four hundred tools. What breaks?
points: Tool descriptions are context tax paid on every call — this becomes a context problem first (#14)
Name collisions across servers; ambiguous overlapping tools; the model picks plausibly and wrongly
Fix by curation: a gateway/registry that exposes a filtered, task-relevant subset per agent
Or route: classify intent → attach only that toolkit's servers (06-AGENTIC-AI #7)
Operational reality: N servers = N failure domains, N version streams, N security reviews
questions.flow: descriptions cost context → curate via gateway → route by intent → accept N failure domains
questions.trap: connecting every available server because you can

questions.text: How do you version a tool contract?
points: A tool signature is a public API — the model's calls are the clients you can't see
Additive optional params are safe; renames, removals and semantic changes are breaking
Semantic change is the sneaky one: same signature, different behaviour → silent wrong actions
Version in the tool name or the server capability; run old and new in parallel through a deprecation window
Regression-test with recorded trajectories (06-AGENTIC-AI #20) — that's your contract test
questions.flow: tool = public API → additive safe → version breaking changes → parallel run → replay trajectories to verify
questions.trap: changing what a tool means while keeping its signature

questions.text: When would you not use MCP?
points: Single app, few fixed tools, one model vendor → native function calling is less machinery
Ultra-low-latency paths — an extra hop and serialisation you don't need
Hard-regulated environments where a new protocol surface means a new audit you can't afford yet
Where the integration is genuinely one-off and will never be reused, portability buys nothing
Honest framing: MCP pays off at fleet scale and across teams, not in a single service
questions.flow: few fixed tools + one vendor → native calling · reuse across teams/agents → MCP
questions.trap: adopting it for a single service because it's the current vocabulary

questions.text: What is context engineering, and why isn't it prompt engineering?
points: Prompt engineering = wording one instruction. Context engineering = deciding what occupies the window at every step
It became a discipline when agents got long: the prompt is now the smallest part of the context
Competing claims on a finite budget: system + tool descriptions + retrieved docs + history + scratchpad + output room
It's a systems problem — selection, ordering, compaction, eviction — not a writing problem
Directly determines cost, latency (prefill) and accuracy simultaneously
questions.badge: Trending — the reframing recurs across engineering blogs + agentic JDs (2025–26)
questions.flow: finite window → many competing claims → select, order, compact, evict → per step, not once
questions.trap: describing it as "writing better prompts"

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_agentic Q15: "'Context engineering' is replacing 'prompt engineering' as the term of art. What actually changed?"
drill.badge: Trending — the reframing recurs across engineering blogs + agentic JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: The unit of design is no longer a string. What are you actually curating per model call, and against what budget?
points: The shift: from crafting a clever instruction to curating everything in the window per call — system prompt, tool schemas, retrieved docs, memory, message history, tool results — as a budgeted portfolio. The prompt is one line-item; the context is the system.

Because attention is a finite budget: irrelevant or stale tokens don't just cost money, they degrade selection and reasoning (distraction, lost-in-the-middle). Curation is subtractive as much as additive.

Concrete techniques to name: retrieval instead of stuffing, summarization/compaction of history, truncating tool outputs with "fetch more" affordances, scoping tools per turn, structured state outside the window with only the relevant slice loaded.

For agents specifically: context is dynamic across the loop — each iteration re-decides what the model needs now, which makes context assembly a runtime component with its own logic and tests, not a template.
The architect's takeaway: most "model is dumb" bugs are context bugs — audit what was actually in the window at the failing step before blaming the model.
drill.oneLiner: Prompt engineering wrote a good instruction; context engineering budgets the whole window — what to retrieve, compress, truncate and exclude per step — because attention is finite and most 'model failures' turn out to be context assembly failures.

questions.text: Budget a 128k window for a real agent.
points: Reserve output room first — the most common self-inflicted failure is no space to answer
Fixed floor: system prompt + tool descriptions (this is why #11 matters)
Variable: retrieved context, conversation history, scratchpad/observations — these must be capped, not hoped
Place critical material at start and end (04-LLM-FOUNDATIONS #22) — the middle degrades
Instrument it: token counts per section, per step. Unbudgeted context is how cost surprises happen
questions.flow: reserve output → fixed floor → cap each variable section → critical material at the edges → measure per step
questions.trap: letting history and observations grow until the model silently truncates

questions.text: Run's at step 40. What do you throw away?
points: Compaction: summarise older turns into a running state object, drop the raw trace
Drop resolved sub-tasks entirely — a completed detour has no further value
Keep: the goal, key decisions, constraints discovered, unresolved threads
Re-retrieve on demand rather than retaining everything (#18)
Compaction is lossy — log what you dropped so a failure is debuggable
questions.flow: summarise old turns → drop resolved work → keep goal/decisions/constraints → re-retrieve as needed
questions.trap: naive truncation of the oldest tokens, which silently deletes the goal

questions.text: Answers get worse the longer the session runs. Diagnose it.
points: Classic context rot — stale observations, dead ends, superseded facts accumulating
Distinguish four causes: rot · dilution (too much irrelevant) · position (lost in middle) · genuine truncation
Diagnose by replay: same query with a fresh context vs the long one — if fresh wins, it's context, not model
Instrument context length and composition against quality metrics per step; the correlation is usually visible
Fixes: compaction (#16), sub-agent isolation (#19), re-retrieval, hard turn caps
questions.flow: replay fresh vs long → isolates context from model → then classify rot / dilution / position / truncation
questions.trap: swapping to a bigger model when a fresh-context replay would have proved it wasn't the model

questions.text: What gets written to memory, and what gets read back?
points: Write policy: after each turn, on explicit signal, or model-decided (remember_this tool) — each has a different failure
Write too much → retrieval noise and cost. Write too little → the agent feels amnesiac
Read policy: retrieve relevant memory per turn — never replay the whole store
Memory needs updating and contradiction handling: a changed preference must supersede, not coexist
Retention and deletion are compliance surface, not just engineering (GDPR/right to be forgotten)
questions.flow: explicit write policy → selective retrieval on read → supersede on contradiction → retention rules
questions.trap: append-only memory that accumulates contradictions and never forgets anything

questions.text: How does sub-agent isolation help context?
points: Sub-agent gets a clean window for its subtask, returns only the result — not its trace
The parent's context stays small; the exploration cost is paid and discarded
This is a real argument for multi-agent that survives the "when multi-agent hurts" critique (06-AGENTIC-AI #14)
Cost: the handoff is lossy — what the sub-agent learned but didn't report is gone
Design the return contract explicitly: what must come back, in what shape
questions.flow: subtask in a fresh window → return result only → parent context stays lean → design the return contract
questions.trap: sub-agents that return their whole transcript, defeating the purpose

questions.text: How does prompt caching change how you order context?
points: Providers cache a prefix — savings only if the front of your context is byte-identical across calls
So: stable content first (system, tool defs, few-shot), volatile content last (retrieved, history)
One changed character early invalidates the whole downstream cache
Big lever on agent loops specifically, where the same prefix re-enters every step
Interacts with #15: the "put critical material at the end" instinct and cache ordering must be reconciled deliberately

links.label: caching in agentic systems
links.target: 03-Agentic-AI/11-Production Agentic Systems (architect lens)/95-caching in agentic systems

questions.flow: stable prefix first → volatile suffix last → never mutate the front → biggest win in loops
questions.trap: injecting a timestamp or request ID into the system prompt and killing every cache hit

questions.text: Multi-tenant. How do you keep context from leaking?
points: Memory and cache keys must include tenant — a shared semantic cache is a cross-customer leak waiting to happen
Retrieval filters enforced server-side at the store, never as a post-filter in application code
Tool credentials scoped to the tenant's own principal (#8), not a shared service account
Prompt-cache prefixes must not contain tenant data if the prefix is shared across tenants
Audit and traces carry tenant ID, or an incident can't be scoped or reported

links.label: Access Control & Security — Per Tenant Retrieval
links.target: 04-RAG/12-Production RAG Systems (arch lens)/08-Access Control & Security — Per-Tenant Retrieval

questions.flow: tenant in every key → server-side retrieval filter → per-tenant creds → tenant-free shared prefixes → tenant on every trace
questions.trap: a semantic answer cache keyed on query text alone

questions.text: How do you version and roll out a prompt change?
points: Prompts are deployable artifacts: versioned in git, reviewed, tagged on every trace
Never edit in a console with no history — untraceable quality regressions are the result
Roll out like code: canary/shadow, compare against a golden set, roll back on regression
Version the whole coupled unit — prompt + tool defs + model version move together, like RAG's index contract
Every response should be attributable to an exact prompt version, or eval is guesswork
questions.badge: Trending — prompt-ops questions recur across LLMOps JDs (2025–26)
questions.flow: prompt in git → tag version on traces → canary against golden set → roll back → version the coupled unit
questions.trap: treating the prompt as config rather than code, and losing attribution

drill.prompt: from jbtiq_llm Q21: "Prompts in production: someone edits one string and quality drops 15% for a week before anyone notices. Fix the process."
drill.badge: Trending — prompt-ops questions recur across LLMOps JDs (2025–26)
drill.hint: Treat the prompt as what it actually is: deployed code with no compiler. What does code get that your prompts don't?
points: The diagnosis: prompts are behavior-defining deployed artifacts being edited like copy text — no versioning, no tests, no review, no observability tying quality to the change.

Version control: prompts in git (or a prompt-management system) with IDs; every trace logs which prompt version served it — otherwise incidents are unattributable. Template/variable separation so data changes aren't logic changes.
Eval gate as CI: a golden set + LLM-judge/assertion suite runs on every prompt PR; a 15% regression fails the merge, not the users. This is the single highest-leverage fix.

Deployment discipline: prompts roll out like code — canary a slice, watch task-success/complaint metrics, roll back a version, A/B when the change is contested. Remember the coupling: prompt and model version pair; re-gate prompts when the model moves.
Cultural point worth voicing: the fix isn't gatekeeping who edits — it's making the safe path the easy path, so PMs can edit prompts because the eval gate catches the damage.
drill.oneLiner: Prompts are deployed code without a compiler — so they get versions logged in every trace, an eval gate in CI that fails regressions before merge, canaried rollouts with rollback, and re-gating whenever the underlying model changes.

questions.text: Retrieve it again, or keep it in context?
points: Retain when it's small, stable and needed every step — the goal, constraints, schema
Re-retrieve when it's large, changeable, or needed occasionally — documents, records, tool results
Retention costs tokens every step and compounds; retrieval costs latency once, when needed
In long runs retrieval almost always wins — retention is what causes rot (#17)
Middle ground: keep a compact pointer/summary in context, fetch the full body on demand
questions.flow: small + always needed → retain · large or occasional → re-retrieve → keep pointers, fetch bodies
questions.trap: keeping every retrieved document in context "in case it's needed again"

questions.text: Design the context layer for a long-running assistant.
points: Tiers: working (this turn) · session (compacted running state) · long-term (retrieved memory store)
Explicit budget per tier with hard caps; compaction on a threshold, not on vibes
Stable-prefix ordering for cache (#20), critical material at the edges (#15)
Tenant-scoped everywhere (#21); prompt and tool versions tagged on every trace (#22)
Observability: tokens per section per step, plus quality metrics — so rot is visible before users report it
questions.flow: three tiers + hard caps → compact on threshold → cache-friendly order → tenant-scoped → measure composition vs quality
questions.trap: a memory design with no eviction, no budget and no measurement

questions.text: Where have you had to engineer context rather than just prompt?
points: Anchor on a real constraint: cost per session, degradation over turns, or a window you kept hitting
What you measured — token composition per step is the detail that proves you did this for real
The lever: compaction, re-retrieval, sub-agent isolation, cache reordering
The trade you accepted — what you dropped and what that cost you
Number: cost per session, quality at turn N, or window-overflow rate, before → after
questions.flow: constraint → measured composition → lever chosen → what you dropped → number
questions.trap: a prompt-wording story dressed up as context engineering
